summary.text: The siege of Jerusalem lasted from 7 June to 15 July 1099 and marked the successful end of the First Crusade.
Christian forces from Western Europe, mobilised by Pope Urban II after the Council of Clermont, attacked a city held first by the Seljuk Turks and later by the Egyptian Fatimids.
After an unsuccessful first attack on 13 June, the crusaders built several siege engines, including a siege tower and a battering ram, and entered the city on 15 July.

paragraphs.heading: The end of the First Crusade
paragraphs.text: From 7 June to 15 July 1099, crusader armies from Western Europe laid siege to Jerusalem. Their victory brought the First Crusade to a successful close, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem was set up soon after. Pope Urban II had called these armies together following the Council of Clermont in 1095. A first assault on 13 June failed, so the crusaders built several siege engines, among them a siege tower and a battering ram, which let them in on 15 July.

paragraphs.heading: The long road south
paragraphs.text: Urban's call in 1095 had two goals: to help Byzantium, which the Seljuks threatened, and to reach the Holy Land and free Jerusalem. The main armies left Constantinople in April 1097 and reached northern Syria that autumn. They besieged Antioch from October 1097 until it fell in June 1098, then beat a Seljuk relief army led by Kerbogha. After that, power struggles between Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond of Toulouse, along with disease and short supplies, held the march up for months. Raymond took command and led the march south in January 1099, reaching Jerusalem on 7 June.

paragraphs.heading: A hard city to take
paragraphs.text: Jerusalem had been out of Christian hands since the Muslim conquest of the Levant in 637. Its walls went back to the emperor Hadrian and had been kept up and strengthened ever since. They ran four kilometres around the city, stood 15 metres high and were three metres thick, with five main gates, each guarded by two towers. Steep valleys protected the east, southeast and west, so only the southwest, across Mount Zion, and the whole length of the northern wall gave attackers good ground.

paragraphs.heading: The governor gets ready
paragraphs.text: On hearing a Christian army was coming, the governor, Iftikhar ad-Dawla, began to prepare. He made sure no water, food or wood was left near the city for the enemy. He drove out Syrian Christians who might side with the crusaders, while letting all Jews stay. Expecting siege engines, he had all the timber and rope he could find turned into more mangonels for the defence, and he had bags stuffed with straw sewn so they could be lowered on ropes beside the walls to soften the blows of flying stones. His garrison was roughly a thousand Arab and Sudanese soldiers plus some 400 elite Egyptian horsemen.

paragraphs.heading: An army short of water
paragraphs.text: Of the 20,000 to 75,000 troops thought to have gathered at Nicaea, between 12,000 and 14,000 reached Jerusalem, including 1,200 to 1,300 cavalry. Most wells and cisterns had been made useless, and heat and lack of shade made the crusaders' thirst worse. Their one source was the Gihon spring, flowing from the city’s southeast spur, which could give over a million litres a day in winter but ran much lower in summer. Inside, people drew on deep cisterns and hundreds of smaller ones under houses, fed by channels from roofs and streets.

paragraphs.heading: Taking up positions
paragraphs.text: The crusaders were too few to surround the whole city, so they massed where they could get close to the walls. Robert of Normandy faced the northern wall, Robert of Flanders stood on his right, and Godfrey of Lorraine held the northwest corner down to the Jaffa Gate, where Tancred joined him. Raymond of Toulouse started in the south, but the valley kept him too far from the walls, so after two or three days he moved up onto Mount Zion. Nobody watched the eastern and southeastern sides.

paragraphs.heading: Failure, then success
paragraphs.text: According to Raymond of Aguilers, an old hermit foretold that the city would fall to an attack on 13 June. The assault began well but failed, which showed that more siege engines were needed. Two days later the leaders met to rethink their plan, accepting that heaven would not hand them the city and that the situation favoured the defenders. The machines they then built carried them inside on 15 July, and afterwards the crusaders massacred thousands of Muslims and Jews.
